summary: Redwood ran an Optimize walkthrough for Starlite Finance focusing on batching strategies, prefix and KV cache recommendations, and an associated cost model. Cache hit rate sensitivity and cost model impact
Dedicated vs hosted economics for sustained throughput

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'll kick us off. quick run through agenda: batching, KV/prefix cache, cost model, then Q&A.
[00:08] Lena (Starlite): Thanks, Maya. We want to understand how much we can save and what the latency trade-offs look like. our users are latency sensitive but costs are getting out of hand.
[00:18] Diego (Redwood SE): yeah, understood. quick clarifying question — are most of your calls short chat completions with stable prefixes, or long single-turn generative prompts?
[00:25] Omar (Starlite): majority are multi-turn chat with a 100-300 token prompt avg, a lot of repeat system prompts and user context that could be cached. session lengths vary.
[00:34] Priya (Starlite CISO): Also, we'll need SOC2 config + KMS details before any pilot.
[00:40] Maya: noted, we'll include security pack. okay Diego, take it away.
[00:46] Diego: cool. starting with batching basics — Redwood's runtime does continuous batching across inflight requests with a configurable batching window. the trade-off: larger windows increase throughput (better gpu utilization) but add latency. we typically see diminishing returns after ~40-60ms for chat workloads. example numbers: batch size 1 -> p50 latency 35ms, batch size 8 -> p50 65ms, but tokens/sec up ~3x. these are illustrative.
[01:20] Omar: those numbers look promising but our SLO is 120ms p95. how does that map to p95 not p50?
[01:28] Diego: good call — p95 tends to grow more with burst variability. with adaptive batching plus latency SLO you can set a hard cap: if latency approaches SLO we flush the batch early, trading off some throughput. in practice with a 120ms SLO we saw 2.5x cost reduction on conversational loads.
[01:50] Lena: can you explain prefix vs KV cache again? some of our team uses the term K V cache and we want to be sure.
[01:58] Diego: yes — prefix cache is a short-term cache for common initial tokens (like system prompt + recent history); KV cache here refers to saving model key-value state between steps for the same session so you avoid recomputing earlier layers. Redwood supports both: prefix caching for textual prefixes + KV caching for preserving transformer activations across calls.
[02:18] Maya: small note — sometimes transcripts or automated captions turn KV cache into "K V cash" in our notes, so ignore that.
[02:25] Omar: what's the realistic hit rate we can expect?
[02:28] Diego: depends — for chat with a lot of repeated system prompts, prefix cache hit rates can be 40-70% for the first few tokens. KV cache hit rate is more session-dependent; for long sessions you can keep the KV cache warm and amortize cost across turns. in our modeling we ran three scenarios: low hit (20%), mid (45%), high (70%). cost savings ranged approx 15% -> 60% depending on model size and token distribution.
[03:02] Lena: can you show the cost model?
[03:05] Diego: yes pulling up the spreadsheet — high level: cost = model_runtime_cost * tokens_processed - savings_from_cached_tokens - batching_efficiency. example: for 100M tokens/mo baseline hosted cost X, with mid hit-rate and batching we model ~40% unit cost reduction. (note: live transcription may mangle numbers)
[03:28] Maya: couple of clarifying points — dedicated vs hosted economics: if you have predictable sustained throughput, dedicated reserved capacity can drop per-token run cost further, but has commit. hosted is flexible for spiky workloads.
[03:44] Omar: what about quantization? we are running 7B - do we get more savings with int8 quant and does that change caching behavior?
[03:52] Diego: quantization lowers runtime cost and memory footprint; it doesn't change KV cache semantics but can affect throughput/latency tradeoffs. with int8 we saw 15-25% lower per-token cost and sometimes slightly higher batch sizes before hitting memory limits.
[04:10] Priya: re security: when KV cache exists, is anything stored on disk? we need to know encryption in transit and at rest, and KMS integration.
[04:18] Maya: good question — Redwood only persists KV cache in-memory on the serving node for the session; for Private deployments there are options to control persistence. keys are managed via customer KMS for Private, and audit logs show cache events. we'll send details in the security pack.
[04:34] Omar: can we get an estimate for our traffic? our 1k concurrent sessions, avg 200 tokens per turn, 3 turns per minute — what does the model say?
[04:42] Diego: we can run that through the spreadsheet; roughly ballpark: 1k conc sessions with those params gives Y tokens/sec — approximate savings with mid 45% hit-rate and batching window tuned: estimate 35-50% reduction in token compute, which maps to similar cost reduction on hosted assuming same per-token price. we'll run exact numbers after we get traces.
[05:05] Lena: about rollout — we can't break prod. how do canaries and fallback work?
[05:09] Diego: Redwood provides canary and A/B rollouts at route level; you can enable caching for a subset of users, monitor quality/regressions via evals, and auto-fallback to a slower model or no-cache path if latencies or error rates spike.
[05:26] Maya: quick demo of the console — (screen share) showing optimize tab, cache hit dashboards, latency percentiles per route, token breakdown per request.
[05:40] [screen share silence / brief pause]
[05:48] Diego: in the console you can set batching window, min batch size, and latency cap; there's also a simulator that runs a trace and shows estimated throughput and cost improvement — that's what we'll ask for from Omar.
[06:06] Omar: nice — will the simulator use our exact model version?
[06:09] Diego: yes, if you provide model config (quantization, sequence length) we can simulate more closely; otherwise we use default profiles for similar architectures.
[06:18] Priya: on compliance — audit logs retention, SSO, RBAC, data residency — can you table the specifics?
[06:24] Maya: yes, we'll send SOC2 + data residency and KMS docs. Private deployment offers stronger controls for residency.
[06:30] Lena: what would you recommend as first pilot?
[06:33] Diego: pilot plan: 2-week pilot on hosted with a 10% traffic canary, run simulator on your trace, tune batching window and prefix cache policies, measure hit-rate and latency. after pilot, evaluate Dedicated if sustained throughput warrants commit.
[06:52] Omar: timeline wise we want numbers by next week for budget.
[06:55] Maya: we'll prioritize the cost-model and simulator run — action items and dates in follow-up.
[07:00] [longer section of Q&A about edge cases]
[07:10] Diego: one nuance: prefix caching helps mostly for the first N tokens (system prompts, static instructions). KV cache avoids recomputing early layers — so for multi-turn chat you get the most benefit when you can reuse the KV between steps. but if users edit past messages a lot, cache invalidation hits will reduce benefit.
[07:34] Lena: interesting — our product edits history a fair bit — how do you handle invalidation?
[07:38] Diego: we support per-session invalidation and partial invalidation if only tail messages change. policies can be tuned: conservative invalidation for safety, or optimistic if edits are rare.
[07:50] Omar: are there any accuracy regressions we should expect when using caching or batching?
[07:54] Diego: caching itself doesn't change model outputs — it only avoids recomputing. batching can affect scheduling but not output deterministically; however some nondeterminism may appear with floating point differences if you change model backend or quantization. we recommend running a small eval set to verify no regressions.
[08:12] Priya: last security question — will cached tokens ever be included in logs? we need PII concerns addressed.
[08:18] Maya: logs are configurable; you can redact or not log prompt content, and audit logs capture cache events but not full cached content by default. we'll include recommended logging config.
[08:29] Lena: ok last thing — can you share example cost numbers for our 3 scenarios?
[08:33] Diego: quick readout from spreadsheet (approx): low hit 20% -> 18% cost reduction; mid 45% -> 38% reduction; high 70% -> 58% reduction. these fold in batching gains and assume current hosted per-token pricing. final numbers will move when you share traces.
[08:55] Omar: that 38% mid-case is compelling.
[08:58] Maya: great. recap: Redwood to share cost model and security pack, Starlite to share traces, Diego to run sim and bench.
[09:08] Priya: we'll review security docs before pilot sign-off.
[09:12] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for benchmark slot.
[09:17] [call ends]
